title: Maximum Height by Stacking Cuboids
statement:
You are given `n` cuboids. Cuboid `i` has three side lengths `a[i]`, `b[i]`, `c[i]`.

You may choose any subset of the cuboids and stack them in a single vertical tower. Each chosen cuboid can be **rotated freely**: you decide which of its three side lengths is its width, which is its length and which is its height. Cuboid `X` may be placed directly on top of cuboid `Y` only if, in the chosen orientations, the width of `X` is at most the width of `Y`, the length of `X` is at most the length of `Y`, and the height of `X` is at most the height of `Y` (all three comparisons, equality allowed). The tower must be stable in this sense for every adjacent pair.

The height of the tower is the sum of the chosen heights. Return the **maximum possible height** of a tower.

Cuboids with identical dimensions are distinct objects, and each cuboid can be used at most once.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
Each of the next `n` lines contains three integers: the side lengths of one cuboid.
outputFormat: Print a single integer, the maximum tower height.

examples.explanation: Lay the first cuboid as width 2, length 3, height 4 and the second as width 1, length 2, height 3. The second fits on the first in all three dimensions, so the tower has height 4 + 3 = 7.

The first cuboid has a side of 10, which exceeds every side of the cube, so it can never sit on the cube. The cube cannot sit on it either, because the cube has no side of length at most 1. The best tower is the first cuboid alone, standing on its 10 side.
All three cuboids nest: 1x1x2 fits on a 2x2x2 cube, and one cube fits on the other. The height is 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.

hints: Rotations make this look like a huge search. Is there an orientation of each cuboid that is always at least as good as the others?
Sort the three sides of every cuboid. If X can sit on Y in some orientations, it can also sit on Y when both are sorted ascending, and the largest side makes the best height.

After sorting each cuboid's sides, sort the cuboids themselves. Then dp[i] = height_i + max(dp[j]) over earlier j with all three sorted sides at most those of i, like a longest increasing subsequence with weights.
